yield_factor_source: engine/county_yield_factors.json: model scaled to the mean USDA NASS dryland yield of the county

units.yield: kg/ha at farm level (trial-level model x county yield factor)
units.net_return: 2025 USD per acre per year, averaged over the whole rotation, fallow acres included; actual Kansas price of each harvest year; K-State budget of the field's cost region, land rent included; crop insurance and government payments excluded. mean_before_land_rent adds the region's rent back (nearly the same for every rotation of a region, within a few dollars)

yield_scenarios._about: The main rotation records above use county_average. well_managed repeats the per-rotation numbers with the yield level of the K-State budgets whose costs are used; the app can swap them in. Description of each: engine/counties.py SCENARIOS.
yield_scenarios.county_average: Average dryland yield of the county (USDA NASS): all farms, good and poor fields, every rotation position

ranking_sensitivity.note: Share of all possible priority weightings under which each rotation ranks first; water and soil share one weight in the draw because they measure nearly the same thing. Below about 0.6 for the leader, the ranking depends on the farmer's priorities.

well_managed.description: Planning yield of the K-State budget whose costs are used: a well-managed field. The costs then match the yields

rotations.name: Wheat - fallow
rotations.why: The traditional dryland system of western Kansas: a 14-month fallow stores water so that wheat survives dry years. It is the baseline every other rotation is compared with.
benefits: Highest stored soil water at wheat planting (about 9.4 in in 8 ft at Tribune, E09)
Simplest system: one crop, one set of equipment
risks: Long bare or residue-only period (wind erosion, loss of organic matter)
Lost money on average in 2008-2015 at Tribune (-$18/acre, E07)
Fallow stores only about 28% of the rain that falls during it (E08)
gaps: How much water fallow really stores on this field (soil-specific; satellites cannot measure it)
Wheat failures from winterkill, disease and hail are not water effects and are not modelled (E15)
Stored soil water on this field is modelled from gridded weather, not measured
Yields are long-run estimates; a single year can be far off, wheat more than sorghum (docs/engine-validation.md)
check_locally: Soil probe depth or soil-water reading at planting
Current crop insurance coverage (excluded from the economics)

rotations.name: Wheat - sorghum - fallow
rotations.why: Adds a drought-tolerant summer crop between wheat and fallow: two crops in three years instead of one in two. Researched in western Kansas for forty years.
benefits: Only rotation with a positive average net return at Tribune 2008-2015 (< $6/acre, E07)
More total grain than wheat-fallow at Colby, Garden City and Tribune (E16)
Shorter fallows store water more efficiently (E16)
Sorghum needs only about 7 in of water use before it makes grain (E17)
risks: Sorghum failed completely in 2002 and 2012 at Tribune (E02)
Less stored water for wheat than after a full fallow (E09)
gaps: Local sorghum price and basis (AMS Market News)
No pest, disease or hail modelling
Stored soil water on this field is modelled from gridded weather, not measured
Yields are long-run estimates; a single year can be far off, wheat more than sorghum (docs/engine-validation.md)
check_locally: Elevator or feedlot buying sorghum nearby, and the basis
Herbicide carry-over between wheat and sorghum

rotations.name: Wheat - corn - fallow
rotations.why: Same structure as wheat-sorghum-fallow but with corn, which pays more per bushel and has a wider market. In Greeley County 17% of wheat fields go to corn the next year (CDL pixel sequences 2010-2024, project brief).
risks: Corn needs about 11 in of water use before it makes grain, sorghum about 7 in (E17)
At Tribune sorghum yielded about twice as much as corn in the same rotation (E11)
gaps: Corn yield in very dry years is close to zero; the distribution matters more than the mean
Stored soil water on this field is modelled from gridded weather, not measured
Yields are long-run estimates; a single year can be far off, wheat more than sorghum (docs/engine-validation.md)
check_locally: Seed and fertiliser cost per acre against the K-State budget

rotations.name: Wheat - sorghum - sorghum - fallow
rotations.why: More intensive: three crops in four years. Tested at Tribune since 1996, so the effect of a second sorghum crop is measured, not guessed.
benefits: Shortest share of time in fallow of the tested rotations
risks: Second sorghum yields about 65% of the first (E05)
About 1.5 in less soil water at planting of the second sorghum (E06)
gaps: No K-State budget for the second sorghum year
Stored soil water on this field is modelled from gridded weather, not measured
Yields are long-run estimates; a single year can be far off, wheat more than sorghum (docs/engine-validation.md)
check_locally: Weed and disease pressure in sorghum after sorghum
Grazing sorghum residue as an extra income

rotations.name: Wheat - wheat - sorghum - fallow
rotations.why: For a farmer who wants to stay mostly in wheat: a second wheat crop replaces part of the fallow. Measured at Tribune since 1996.
benefits: Three crops in four years with familiar wheat equipment
risks: Recrop wheat yields about 75% of the first wheat (E03)
About 3 in (40%) less soil water at recrop-wheat planting (E06)
Wheat-on-wheat raises disease and grassy-weed risk (check locally)
gaps: No K-State budget for recrop wheat in southwest Kansas
Stored soil water on this field is modelled from gridded weather, not measured
Yields are long-run estimates; a single year can be far off, wheat more than sorghum (docs/engine-validation.md)
check_locally: Wheat streak mosaic and volunteer wheat control between crops

rotations.name: Wheat - sunflower - fallow
rotations.why: A summer crop with the lowest water threshold in the K-State functions (about 5.4 in, E17) and its own K-State budget for western Kansas (E26).
benefits: Lowest threshold ET of the tested crops (E17)
Deep roots use water below the wheat root zone (FAO-56 root depth 0.8-1.5 m, E25)
risks: Little residue left after harvest: more erosion risk during the next fallow (ASSUMPTION, residue_class 'low')
Smaller and more distant markets than wheat or sorghum
gaps: No Tribune year-by-year sunflower yields to validate against
Residue effect on the next fallow is not quantified
Stored soil water on this field is modelled from gridded weather, not measured
Yields are long-run estimates; a single year can be far off, wheat more than sorghum (docs/engine-validation.md)
check_locally: Nearest crusher or buyer for oil sunflower

rotations_not_modelled.WS-forage: no yield function for one of its crops

default_weights_note: water and soil both measure cropping intensity (indicators correlate 0.95), so together they weigh as much as one money criterion: income 2, dry_year_safety 2, water 1, soil 1

ranking_sensitivity.note: Share of all possible priority weightings under which each rotation ranks first; water and soil share one weight in the draw because they measure nearly the same thing. Below about 0.6 for the leader, the ranking depends on the farmer's priorities.

scoring_note: income and dry_year_safety: net return minus that of wheat-fallow (WF) on this field and scenario, USD/acre/yr

farm_factor._source: wheat, sorghum: calibration_targets.csv T19 and T20 (county / trial yields); corn, sunflower: ASSUMPTION, same as sorghum

assumptions: Every phase of a rotation is present every year (land split evenly between phases)
Costs before 2016 equal the mean real 2016-2026 K-State budget cost (crops-economics/HANDOVER.md, A2)

Average yield level of each crop = mean USDA NASS dryland yield of the county (1996 onward); the model supplies the year-to-year variation. Costs come from K-State budgets for a well-managed field, so this main scenario favours fallow; see yield_scenarios.well_managed
Corn and sunflower have no trial calibration; their level comes only from county yields. Corn at Hays is the least certain number
Sorghum at the 1996-2020 average yield level; measured trial yields rose by about 2 bu/acre per year, so today's sorghum is probably understated
The model stores less water in a 14-month fallow than measured at Tribune, so wheat-fallow is probably somewhat better than shown
Scores use fixed scales chosen by the team; they are value judgements
Differences of a few dollars per acre between rotations are inside the model's error
